Are new research just a recycle of old ideas in a new context?
docs.text:
A question I keep coming back to: when something feels new in research, how much of it is genuinely new, and how much is an old idea wearing the clothes of a new context?

Attention wasn't invented in 2017 — alignment models in machine translation were already doing soft lookups years before. Backprop is 1980s. Even "in-context learning" rhymes with ideas about analogy and case-based reasoning that are decades old. What changed was the context: more compute, more data, a different substrate to run the old idea on.

Maybe that's the point. An idea is cheap; the context that makes it work is expensive. The recycle isn't lazy — moving an idea into a context where it finally pays off is itself the contribution. The transformer paper's value wasn't "attention exists," it was "attention, alone, at this scale, is enough."

So the honest answer is probably: yes, mostly recycled — but recycling into the right context is most of what progress actually is. The rare truly-new idea is the exception, and even it stands on a stack of recontextualized old ones.

Worth keeping in mind next time I feel like I haven't had an "original" idea: the value might be in spotting which old idea belongs in this new context.
